name: the beach
title: A Grey Beach
description: Before you stretches a desolate strand of damp sand, strewn with broken shells and the refuse of the tide. A persistent wind sweeps in from the sea.
The grey beach extends beneath a restless sky. Shell fragments lie among the seaweed deposited by the last tide, and the wind affords scarcely a moment's respite.
On one side lies the open sea; on the other, dunes of pale sand. Between them runs a narrow shore marked by wrack and shells, where the wind is never quite still.
_map: position on the route map (grid cells); the camp (travelHours 0) has a path to every place
_arrive: what you see each time you come back: every line whose 'when' holds, in order

text: The familiar beach opens before you, and the salt wind meets you at once.
You emerge upon the shore once more, where sand and wind appear unchanged.
The sea comes into view, and with it the beach exposed to every passing gust.
You return to the damp strand, its tide line darkened by seaweed.
The beach presents its customary aspect: wet sand, scattered shells, and a line of wrack.
Beneath your feet the sand is firm with moisture; the tide has left its debris in a winding line.
Darkness has concealed the beach, though each breaking wave shows a pale crest of foam.
At night the coast can scarcely be distinguished; only wind and surf betray the direction of the sea.
The shore lies obscure beneath the night sky, save where the surf traces a faint white line.
A thread of smoke rises from the circle of rocks, marking the living hearth.
Smoke ascends steadily above the stones and is scattered by the wind.
The fire still burns within the sheltering rocks.
The hearth among the rocks is cold and silent.
Only cold ashes occupy the ring of stones.
No smoke rises from the rocks; the fire has expired.
Shellfish remain attached to the wet rock beneath the cliff.
The stones at the cliff's foot are still crowded with shells.
Beneath the cliff, the shellfish lie exposed until the returning tide.
Small fish flash in the shallow water beside the shore.
An occasional silver movement betrays fish among the shallows.
The school of fish continues to frequent the water near the beach.

explore.name: look around
explore._explore: look around: a pop-up with what you see (view lines whose 'when' holds) and the landmarks not explored yet; no time passes until you pick one

text: The grey strand stretches in either direction until it disappears beyond the bends of the coast. Broken shells and long banks of wrack mark the reach of the tide.
From this point you can follow the empty beach with your eyes for some distance. Its upper margin is strewn with shells and seaweed.
Sand and fragments cast up by the waves cover the shore; beyond its distant curves, the course of the coastline remains unknown.

view.text: Beyond the dunes you distinguish a continuous dark belt of trees.
Beyond the sandy ridges begins the forest, its foliage closing over the inland ground.
At the farther extremity of the beach, dark rocks stand together in an irregular ring.
The cluster of rocks at the end of the shore offers a refuge from the prevailing wind.
A thin column of smoke rises above the rocks and disperses in the sea breeze.
Past the rocks, a low cliff ends abruptly in the surf.
Molluscs cling in numbers to the wet stone beneath the cliff.
The face of the cliff is steep, though a securely fastened rope might make its ascent possible.
Beyond the cliff, towards the west, the ground opens into broad meadows.
An occasional silver flash betrays movement in the shallow water.
A school of small fish turns and scatters among the shallows.

nothingLeft: A further survey of the shore reveals no feature overlooked before.
By now the principal features of this stretch of coast are familiar to you.
The tide may bring other things in time, but today the shore yields no new discovery.

landmarks.label: the dunes
text: You climb the loose sand of the dunes, gaining a better view of the country. Behind the crest the coast gives way to a dense forest, near enough to reach on foot; whether it offers fresh water or useful timber remains to be learned.
From the summit of the dunes you observe a line of tall trees on the landward side. The forest begins within a short walk, promising shade and perhaps a different class of resources.
The climb is laborious in the soft sand, but it reveals the first distinct feature of the island's interior: a forest, scarcely an hour's walk away.
landmarks.journal: You discover a forest beyond the dunes.

landmarks.label: the ring of rocks
text: At the end of the beach, a natural ring of rocks breaks the full force of the sea wind. Its enclosed ground would serve admirably for a bed, and a hearth could be established there with little labour.
The formation proves more useful on inspection than from a distance. The rocks shut out much of the wind, leaving a space in which to sleep and maintain a campfire.
Between the boulders you find a sheltered hollow. Nature has supplied the walls; a bed and a fire would be enough to make it a serviceable first camp.
landmarks.journal: You find sheltered ground among the rocks.

landmarks.label: the low cliff
text: Beneath a low cliff the retreating tide exposes stones thickly covered with shellfish. They may be eaten raw, though heat would render this modest resource more nourishing.
The wet rock at the cliff's foot is occupied by countless shells. Here, at least, the sea offers food without the need for a boat; it would be better still when cooked.
You examine the cliff and discover an accessible bed of shellfish upon the stones below. They promise an immediate meal, and a better one if a fire can be made.
landmarks.journal: You find shellfish clinging to the cliff rocks.

landmarks.label: the shallows
text: A school of small fish moves through the shallows in quick, coordinated turns. Too swift for the unaided hand, they might nevertheless be taken with a properly sharpened spear.
The water is shallow enough to wade, and fish are plentiful; but their movements are exceedingly rapid. A pointed stick would greatly improve your chances.
Silver bodies dart through the clear water close to shore. The fish cannot be grasped by hand, but they remain within reach of a spear.
landmarks.journal: Fish gather in the shallows. A spear might catch them.

landmarks.label: climb the cliff
text: Having secured the rope about a firm boulder, you ascend the cliff with considerable caution. From its summit the western country comes into view: a broad expanse of grassland, dotted with bushes and willows, perhaps an hour's walk away.
The rope bears your weight as you climb the steep face. At the top you discover what the cliffs had concealed: meadows extending westward, their long grasses stirred by the wind.
The ascent is short, but there is little secure footing. Once above the cliff, you observe a new region to the west, where meadows sweep towards a line of willows about an hour distant.
landmarks.journal: From the cliff, you discover meadows to the west.
landmarks.requiresText: Too steep to climb without a rope

activities.name: light fire
log: A match flares beneath your hands; the dry fibres begin to smoke and presently take fire.
You shelter the tiny flame from the wind until it passes to the kindling.
With a carefully struck match, you kindle the prepared wood.
activities._note: with matches: 15 min, always works, one match each time

activities.name: light fire
activities._note: without matches, with 2 stones: sparks, 1 h, catches 2 times in 3; the stones stay; the wood is only used when it catches
log: You strike the stones repeatedly over a nest of dry grass, seeking a spark that will persist.
Sparks fall upon the tinder, but most vanish before they can set it alight.
Patient blows of stone against stone produce brief sparks, while the effort leaves your knuckles sore.

text: At last one of the sparks lodges in the tinder. A cautious breath enlarges the glow into a flame.
The dry fibres begin to smoke; an instant later a small flame rises among them.
A single spark persists long enough to kindle the grass. You feed it slender twigs until the fire is secure.
The sparks expire upon the tinder almost as soon as they fall. The attempt has failed, but the materials remain.
A little smoke appears, then vanishes. The wood is still fit for another trial.
Repeated blows yield nothing but fleeting sparks, and your hands are numbed by the effort.

activities.name: light fire
activities._note: without matches or 2 stones: friction with 2 dry sticks (firewood), 1 h, catches 2 times in 3; the wood (3 to burn, 2 sticks) is only used when it catches
log: You revolve a dry stick against the wood beneath it, working until the friction heats your palms.
Without matches, you turn a slender stick between your hands until your arms grow weary.
The wood is rubbed steadily upon itself, and every trace of smoke is nursed with a cautious breath.

text: A dark ember forms in the powdered wood. Carefully nursed with air and tinder, it becomes a flame.
The faint smoke increases, and a glowing coal at last sets fire to the dry fibres.
Your persistence is rewarded: a small flame rises from the tinder, and you add fuel with great care.
Smoke appears, but the wood never reaches the heat required for flame. It may be tried again.
The forming ember is extinguished before it can kindle the grass. The materials are not lost.
At length fatigue compels you to stop; the sticks have yielded no fire.

activities.name: stoke fire
log: The new fuel catches, and the hearth crackles steadily.
The flames rise higher above the stones.
You add dry wood, and the fire responds with renewed vigour.
Sparks ascend into the darkening air.
A shower of sparks is carried upwards by the wind.
Fresh wood catches with a sudden hiss of escaping moisture.

activities.name: collect shells
log: You prise the shellfish from the rocks as the surf washes around your legs.
Working against the wet stone, you detach the shells while waves break at your knees.
One shell after another comes free, though the cold soon numbs your fingers.
You gather a handful of shells, heavy with seawater.
The day's collection begins with a pocketful of fresh shellfish.
You carry away shells still dripping from the tide.

activities.name: pick up stones
log: At the cliff's foot you examine stones of several kinds, choosing those hardest to the touch.
You select flat, weighty stones from the debris beneath the cliff.
The fallen rock provides stones suitable for rough tools and a hearth.
activities._note: stones lie under the cliff: 2 strike sparks for a fire; also for the rock knife, the axe, the hoe and the weir

activities.name: catch fish

text: Two fish lie upon the sand, taken by successive strokes of the spear.
Your patience has secured two fish from the shallow water.
Two small fish struggle briefly upon the shore: a useful return for the effort.
A single fish is taken. It will provide at least one meal.
The spear rises with one fish upon its point.
Your effort produces one fish, a modest but welcome catch.
The fish turn aside before the spear can reach them.
At each movement the school disperses into deeper water.
The water clouds around the spear, which returns without a catch.

log: You wade cautiously into the shallows with the spear held ready.
Standing knee-deep in cold water, you wait for the fish to approach.
With the spear prepared, you advance slowly through the water.

activities.name: sleep
activities._thoughts: before sleeping: how tired you are (energy, same bands as the bar), then up to 3 things you remember from today, most memorable first

text: You lie down so utterly exhausted that thought is beyond your power.
Fatigue has mastered you; scarcely have you stretched out before your eyes close.
Your remaining strength deserts you, leaving only the desire for sleep.
You rest upon the bed, conscious of an ache in every muscle.
Weariness settles heavily upon your limbs after the day's exertions.
You draw yourself into a more comfortable position, though your whole body protests.
You lie down beneath the weight of a long day's labour.
A slow fatigue overtakes you as you stretch out upon your bed.
With the day's work behind you, a welcome heaviness draws you towards sleep.
You retire while still wakeful, uncertain whether sleep will soon visit you.
You close your eyes and listen to the island, waiting for tiredness to come.
Your strength is not yet spent, and for some time you lie awake.

intro: In the quiet before sleep, the day's discoveries return to your mind.
You review in turn the small events which have occupied the day.
The day's labours present themselves again to your memory.
Lying awake, you consider what your efforts have gained.
The silence invites reflection upon the country around you.
Before sleep, you recall the observations and exertions of the day.

text: You remember the cold sea and the uncertain moment when you first woke on the sand.
The deserted shore and your solitary awakening return vividly to mind.
Again you see the empty horizon where your vessel should have been.
The knife shaving the point of a spear comes back to you.
You recall the care with which the blade was used to shape a straight branch.
The newly fashioned spear, keen beneath your thumb, is a modest satisfaction.
You remember how slowly the stone knife cut into the wood.
The crude blade demanded patience before the branch acquired its point.
A simple spear, formed with a stone edge, seemed a substantial achievement.
You recall the many hours spent grinding a useful edge upon stone.
The sound of stone against stone still seems to linger in your ears.
The crude knife cost more labour than its appearance could suggest.
You picture the fish turning like flashes of silver beneath the water.
The quick movements of the fish in the shallows occupy your thoughts.
Those small fish remain tantalisingly near the shore, yet difficult to take.
Log by log, the shelter rose beside the rocks; you remember the labour well.
You recall the quiet within the shelter after the wind had been excluded.
The walls you raised now meet the force of the sea breeze in your place.
You think with satisfaction of the field's first harvest.
The ripe ears of corn, separated from their stalks, return to memory.
You remember carrying away an armful of grain grown upon the island.
The work of felling timber with the axe remains fresh in your arms.
You recall the axe's repeated blows upon the standing wood.
The acquisition of sound logs seemed another step towards a proper settlement.
You remember standing in the breaking surf with the spear held ready.
The chill of the shallow sea about your knees returns to mind.
You recall waiting motionless for a fish to venture within reach.
The view from the cliff top comes back to you: broad grasslands inland.
You remember the wind upon the summit, and the meadows below.
The difficult ascent revealed a green country beyond the barren shore.
The clear river beneath the willows remains vivid in memory.
You remember the cold current passing rapidly over its stones.
You picture the fish poised in the sheltered pools of the river.
You recall wading into the river, careful of your footing.
The pull of the current upon your legs seemed strongest while you waited.
Beneath the willows you hunted fish in the slower reaches of the stream.
The little flame of a match returns to mind, followed by the welcome warmth.
You remember how readily the kindling caught from a single match.
A faint sulphurous smell, then the odour of burning wood: such was the beginning of the fire.
You recall the painful friction of wood against wood before the first flame appeared.
The long work of turning dry sticks seemed almost without end.
Your sore palms and the small first ember are not easily forgotten.
The blows of stone upon stone at last produced a spark which endured.
You remember the tinder beginning to smoke, then yielding a flame.
Your knuckles still bear witness to the labour of kindling fire with stones.
The cold spring among the mossy rocks rises again in memory.
You remember the astonishing freshness of the water at the spring.
The taste of water drawn straight from the stones is a welcome recollection.
You remember the circle of rocks that shelters your camp from the wind.
The stillness within the rocky enclosure remains a precious comfort.
Among the boulders you found a natural refuge from the weather.
The cool shade beneath the forest canopy returns to you.
You picture the forest, dim and quiet beneath its branches.
The straight trunks and damp scent of moss remain vivid in memory.
You recall the meadow grasses bending in the wind.
The broad sky above the open grassland comes again before your eyes.
You picture pale grasses rolling in waves across the hills.
The berry juice staining your fingers returns to mind.
You remember the sharp thorns as you gathered the small fruit.
The berries' first tartness, then their sweetness, is easily recalled.
You remember the welcome scent of food cooking beside the fire.
The heat of the stones and the smell of roasting provisions return to you.
A simple meal prepared over the fire seemed no small luxury.
You recall collecting bundle after bundle of fallen branches.
The long walk through the woods with fuel upon your arms returns to mind.
Even now you seem to feel the bark and twigs scratching your skin.
The stubborn shellfish clinging to the tide-wet stone come back to mind.
You remember prising the shells loose with fingers numbed by cold.
Again you feel the surf breaking around your legs while you worked.
You remember how welcome the first fresh water tasted.
The thought of clear water refreshes even your memory of the day's labour.
You recall a long drink of clean, cold water.
You remember your modest meal, enough at least to carry you onward.
However plain the food, it was a necessary provision against hunger.
You recall eating what the island afforded, grateful that it was sufficient.

otherwise: Nothing remarkable has marked the day, but even such hours belong to the struggle for survival.
The day's events fade together, leaving little beyond the memory of wind and labour.
There is scant discovery to record: only the sand, the wind, and the passing hours.
The island revealed no novelty today, though its familiar demands remained.
It has been a quiet day, with few events worthy of the journal.
For many hours you have attended to small necessities beneath the ceaseless wind.
thoughts._lines: most memorable first; the fire and the spear are remembered the way you did them (matches, stones or friction; knife or rock knife)

log: At length sleep overcomes you.
Your eyelids grow heavy, and the day's concerns fall silent.
Presently the world fades into darkness.
The long-expected rest arrives.
Sleep comes more swiftly than you had supposed.
You sink into a deep and welcome sleep.
activities._afterwards: the night itself is quiet; on waking: the engine announces the new day and sleep quality, then one line on how your body is (worst first), then the fire

text: You awake trembling and weak; the night has exacted a heavy price.
The effort of sitting upright sets your hands shaking.
Your strength is so diminished that even rising proves difficult.
Hunger and thirst make themselves felt together, with unpleasant urgency.
An empty stomach and a dry mouth are the first sensations of the morning.
You wake in immediate need of both food and water.
Your tongue is dry, and swallowing has become difficult.
An oppressive thirst leaves your throat as dry as the sand.
Before daylight is fully established, thirst has already awakened you.
A persistent ache in the stomach reminds you how little you have eaten.
Hunger is your first concern upon waking.
Your empty stomach demands attention before any other labour.
Cold has left your limbs stiff and reluctant to move.
The night's chill seems to have settled in your joints.
You awake shivering in the morning air.
You awake refreshed and fit for the day's work.
The night's rest has restored a welcome measure of strength.
For once, you rise with strength enough for the coming day.
You have slept, yet the fatigue of yesterday has not wholly disappeared.
Despite the night's rest, your limbs remain heavy.
The hours of sleep have afforded less relief than you had hoped.
The fire continues to smoulder within the circle of stones.
A faint red glow survives among the embers.
A little smoke still rises from the hearth, which has endured the night.
The hearth has been extinguished; nothing remains but cold ash.
Where the fire burned, a pale heap of ashes is now cold.
Not a trace of smoke rises from the dead hearth.
The fire exhausted its fuel during the night.
At some hour before dawn, the last embers went out.
The fuel did not suffice to keep the fire alive until morning.
